reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by defective function of cystinosin, the lysosomal membrane transporter that exports cystine, encoded by the CTNS gene
Rather than an enzyme deficiency, it is a transporter defect, so cystine accumulates and crystallises within lysosomes throughout the body
The classic infantile nephropathic form presents in the first year with renal Fanconi syndrome, causing polyuria, dehydration, electrolyte loss, rickets, and failure to thrive
Corneal cystine crystals are a characteristic finding on slit-lamp examination and cause photophobia over time
Without treatment, progressive kidney disease advances to end-stage renal failure in childhood
Later extrarenal complications include hypothyroidism, growth failure, myopathy, diabetes, and central nervous system involvement
Intermediate (juvenile) and non-nephropathic (ocular) forms have milder or predominantly ophthalmological features
Cystine-depleting therapy with cysteamine slows systemic damage, and topical cysteamine addresses corneal crystals, alongside supportive management of Fanconi losses
reference.pathophysiology: Cystinosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in CTNS, which encodes cystinosin, the transporter that moves cystine out of the lysosome. Impaired transport leads to intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal formation in cells across many tissues, including the kidney, cornea, thyroid, muscle, pancreas, and brain. In the kidney, damage to the proximal tubule produces a generalised reabsorptive defect (Fanconi syndrome) and, over time, progressive glomerular and interstitial injury leading to renal failure. Continued crystal accumulation elsewhere accounts for the later multisystem complications.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome such as Lowe syndrome or mitochondrial disease
Dent disease and other proximal tubular disorders
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of leukocyte cystine content, the key diagnostic and monitoring test
Slit-lamp examination for corneal cystine crystals
Renal function, electrolytes, and urinalysis to characterise Fanconi syndrome
Assessment of growth, thyroid function, and other endocrine and organ involvement
redFlags: Progressive decline in renal function toward end-stage disease
Severe electrolyte disturbance or dehydration from tubular losses
Emerging endocrine, muscular, or neurological complications
reference.prognosis: Untreated nephropathic cystinosis progresses to end-stage renal failure in childhood with multisystem complications. Early and sustained cystine-depleting therapy with supportive care substantially delays renal deterioration and reduces extrarenal complications, improving long-term survival, though adherence is critical and complications may still accrue over time.
pitfalls: Overlooking cystinosis as a cause of Fanconi syndrome and rickets in a young child
Failing to examine for corneal crystals that support the diagnosis
Underestimating the importance of adherence to cystine-depleting therapy and electrolyte replacement
Assuming renal transplantation cures the disorder, when extrarenal cystine accumulation continues
management: Begin lifelong cystine-depleting therapy with oral cysteamine as early as possible to lower intralysosomal cystine, delaying renal decline and extrarenal complications
Prescribe topical cysteamine eye drops for corneal cystine crystals and associated photophobia
Replace the losses of renal Fanconi syndrome with generous fluids, bicarbonate, phosphate, potassium and vitamin D or phosphate supplementation for rickets
Manage progression to end-stage renal failure with dialysis and kidney transplantation, noting the disorder does not recur in the graft
Treat accruing extrarenal complications with levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, insulin for diabetes and growth hormone for growth failure
Titrate cysteamine dosing against serial leukocyte cystine concentration, the key monitoring test
Provide genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive CTNS disorder with family screening, and coordinate metabolic medicine and nephrology
